routes.title: Automorphic bundles and classical automorphic forms, Part II: integral coherent cohomology and Hecke-equivariant perfect complexes
routes.brief: This entry joins the Part II that PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18 proposes and PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-20, PAPER-PILLONI-20 and PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26 join, under the same id, parent (Automorphic bundles and classical automorphic forms, AutomorphicBundles) and title; the design job merges the briefs. It adds one statement, from Scholze, 'On torsion in the cohomology of locally symmetric varieties', Ann. of Math. 182 (2015), §5.1, pp. 1031–1033 (published numbering): for F totally real or CM, G = Res_{F^+/ℚ}Sp_{2n} or the quasisplit unitary group of a form of GL_{2n}, a neat level K and k > n (resp. k ≥ n), the Hecke eigensystems of the prime-to-S Hecke algebra 𝕋 on the holomorphic cusp forms H^0(X*_K, ω_K^{⊗k} ⊗ ℐ) of weight k on the minimal compactification are exactly those of cuspidal automorphic representations π of G with π_∞ ≅ π_k, the holomorphic discrete series of Proposition 5.1.1 (routed to AutomorphicFormsOnReductiveGroups AF.1/AF.4), and 𝕋 acts semisimply there, by the Petersson inner product. This is the same cusp-form-to-automorphic-representation dictionary that the joined proposals already send here (CG20's automorphic-representation-of-eigenform, PILLONI-20's holomorphic-cusp-forms-embed-in-H0, BOXER-PILLONI-26's cuspidal items); plan it once, for the Siegel and unitary Hodge-type data. Import AutomorphicBundles B3–B5 (sections of the canonical and subcanonical extensions), ShimuraCompactifications for the minimal compactification, and AutomorphicFormsOnReductiveGroups AF.1/AF.4 for π_k. Test: n = 1, where G = SL_2 over F^+ and the statement is the classical dictionary for holomorphic Hilbert cusp forms of parallel weight k ≥ 2.
routes.reason: AutomorphicBundles B4 plans classical forms as sections of the canonical and subcanonical extensions, including Siegel and unitary PEL data, but no layer identifies their Hecke eigensystems with cuspidal automorphic representations with prescribed archimedean component; AutomorphicFormsOnReductiveGroups, which sits upstream of every Shimura-variety roadmap, cannot state it. Four accepted extractions already send this dictionary to the proposed Part II IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes, so the item joins it rather than proposing a second owner. Added in review (REV-PAPER-SCHOLZE-15).

The proof of Theorem 4.2.1 uses Scholze's primitive comparison theorem (Scholze 2013, 'p-adic Hodge theory for rigid-analytic varieties', Theorem 5.1) in its compactly supported torsion form on the minimal compactification. The accepted routes of PAPER-SCHOLZE-13 (route 1) and PAPER-ZAVYALOV-25 (route 7) already send the primitive comparison theorem to PadicHodgeTheory P8, and the PadicHodgeTheory P7 packet records that no stage owns Scholze 2013 §5 yet; the fixes for RT-AREA-padic-1/24 propose the early stage PadicHodgeTheory:P8:primitive for it. The compactly supported form used here belongs with it. Added in review (REV-PAPER-SCHOLZE-15).

ALS.5 compares Betti, de Rham and relative Lie algebra cohomology of arithmetic locally symmetric spaces in characteristic zero and consumes AutomorphicSpectralTheory AS.5 for the comparison with automorphic forms. Clozel's result, used in the proof of Corollary 5.4.2, that a regular L-algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n contributes to the cuspidal cohomology of X_K with the coefficient system of its infinitesimal character, is that comparison for GL_n; AutomorphicFormsOnReductiveGroups AF.4 supplies the cohomological representations. Added in review (REV-PAPER-SCHOLZE-15).

review.reason:
The quote matches p. 957 and arXiv v2 p. 15.

The counterexample in the reason works:
- Take R^+ as the integral closure of 𝒪_K + R°°. Its image in R°/R°° = k[T^{1/p^∞}] is integral over k, so it lies in k, and T ∉ R^+.
- R°/R^+ is killed by m_K, so R^+ → R° is almost surjective.
- The rank-two specialization x of the Gauss point with |T(x)| = 1^+ lies in Spa(R, R^+) but not in Spa(R, R°). So the image of Spa(R, R°) → Spa(R, R^+) is not even closed, while V(ker) = V(0) is everything.

The correction matches ECD v4 Definition 5.7(ii), which I read.

One point for the lead. The parenthetical 'The paper applies the notion only with S^+ = S°' is not something the paper states. It should read instead: every use (Corollary 3.2.20, Lemma 2.2.9(ii), Theorem 3.3.18(ii), Theorem 4.1.1(ii), §4.2 p. 1022) concerns a map that is already a Zariski closed embedding built by Lemma 2.2.2 (a boundary, or a pullback of one). So the false implication 'strongly Zariski closed ⇒ Zariski closed' is never used downstream.

sourceIssues.printed: For a subset J ⊂ {1, …, 2g} having cardinality g, the source defines the projective homogeneous coordinate s_J and the open affinoid Fl_J ⊂ Fl by |s_{J′}| ≤ |s_J| for every J′. It asserts transitive permutation of these Fl_J by GSp_{2g}(ℤ_p). On p. 1014 it says stability of the desired property under GSp_{2g}(ℚ_p) gives it on Fl_{g+1,…,2g} and hence every Fl_J.
sourceIssues.reason:
Why the transitivity fails. Take g = 2, coordinates (a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2) with ψ = Σ(a_i b′_i − a′_i b_i), and J = {1,2} versus J′ = {1,3}.
- For W ∈ Fl(ℚ_p) with primitive integral Plücker vector, W ∈ Fl_J iff s_J(W̄) ≠ 0 in 𝔽_p, i.e. iff W̄ is transversal to the complementary coordinate plane.
- The complement of {1,2} is span(e_3,e_4), a Lagrangian. Exactly p³ Lagrangians W̄ ⊂ 𝔽_p^4 are transversal to it (graphs of symmetric maps).
- The complement of {1,3} is span(e_2,e_4), a symplectic plane. Of the (p+1)(p²+1) Lagrangians of 𝔽_p^4, exactly (p+1)² meet it: each meets it in one of its p+1 lines ℓ, and ℓ lies in p+1 Lagrangians. That leaves p³ − p.
- GSp_4(ℤ_p) acts compatibly with reduction, and LG(ℤ_p) → LG(𝔽_p) is surjective. So no γ ∈ GSp_4(ℤ_p) carries Fl_{12} onto Fl_{13}, although Fl_{13} is nonempty (W = span((1,0,0,1),(0,1,1,0)) is Lagrangian with |s_{13}| = |s_{12}| = 1 = max).

Why the Lagrangian Fl_J cover Fl. Every Lagrangian over a field is transversal to one of the 2^g coordinate Lagrangians. Applied to the reduction of a normalised Plücker vector over the valuation ring of a point, this shows that the maximum of |s_J| is always attained at a Lagrangian J.

Where the proof breaks. The last step of the proof of (i) ('and then for all Fl_J') reaches only the orbit of Fl_{g+1,…,2g}, i.e. the Lagrangian J. I did not decide whether 𝒱_J is affinoid perfectoid for non-Lagrangian J: Fl_{13} is a finite union of rational pieces of Lagrangian Fl_{J′}, but that does not make its preimage affinoid. The same restriction applies to Theorem 4.1.1(i), Lemma 4.3.3 and the proof of Theorem 4.3.1, which rest on Theorem 3.3.18(i); since the 2^g Lagrangian charts cover Fl, every later use goes through (found independently by two review readers).

sourceIssues.correction:
Only the inclusion ⊇ holds in general. Equality holds when x^{p^m} ∈ p^{1−ε}R′ implies x ∈ p^{(1−ε)/p^m}R′, for example when R′ is integrally closed in R′[1/p] (R′ = 𝒪_K).

Then the universal point of C gives a point of A[p^m]/C′ over the p-adically complete flat R-algebra 𝒪(C). That point vanishes modulo p^{1−ε}, so it is 0, and C ⊂ C′.
sourceIssues.reason:
Counterexample:
- Take R = 𝒪_C, A = E_{𝒪_C} for an ordinary elliptic curve E over ℤ_p, ε = 0 (Ha is invertible) and m = 1. Then C_1 = E[p]° ≅ μ_p.
- Take R′ = {(a,b) ∈ 𝒪_C × 𝒪_C : a ≡ b mod p^{1/(p−1)}}. It is flat, and p-adically complete, since p²(𝒪_C)² ∩ R′ ⊂ pR′ and R′ is closed.
- s = (ζ_p, 1) ∈ μ_p(R′) = C_1(R′), because v(ζ_p − 1) = 1/(p−1).
- s ≡ 0 mod p^{1/p} would need (ζ_p − 1, 0) ∈ p^{1/p}R′, i.e. v((ζ_p − 1)/p^{1/p}) = 1/(p−1) − 1/p ≥ 1/(p−1). That is false. The example also works for p = 2.

The failing step is the extraction of p^m-th roots: F^m(s) = 0 modulo p^{1−ε} says that the coordinates x of s satisfy x^{p^m} ∈ p^{1−ε}R′.

sourceIssues.locator: §3.2.2, proof of Theorem 3.2.15, p. 986 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Theorem III.2.15, p. 40. This is the sentence of E4; this entry concerns 'locally free', not the degree.
sourceIssues.printed: The source concludes that F̃_{𝔛(p^{−1}ε)} and F̃_{𝔄(p^{−1}ε)} are finite, locally free maps of degree g(g + 1)/2.
sourceIssues.correction: F̃_{𝔛(p^{−1}ε)} and F̃_{𝔄(p^{−1}ε)} are finite, and they become finite locally free (indeed finite étale) of degrees p^{g(g+1)/2} and p^{g(g+1)/2+g} after inverting p. For 0 < ε < 1/2 they are not flat. For ε = 0 they are finite locally free.
sourceIssues.reason:
Work modulo the maximal ideal of ℤ_p^cycl. This ideal contains p^{1−ε}, so F̃ there is the relative-Frobenius-type map of Lemma 3.2.14:
- For ε > 0 it goes from Spec R̄[u]/(u·Ha) to Spec R̄[u′]/(u′·Ha), where R̄ is smooth of dimension d = g(g+1)/2.
- It is Frobenius on R̄ and sends u′ ↦ u^p.

Take a point y with Ha(y) = 0 and u′(y) = 0. Let R′ be the Frobenius fibre, of length p^d, with Ha ∈ its maximal ideal. The fibre over y is R′[u]/(uHa, u^p) = R′ ⊕ ⊕_{i=1}^{p−1}(R′/Ha)u^i, of length ≥ p^d + p − 1.

Over an ordinary point of the same component {u′ = 0} the fibre is R′, of length p^d. That component is connected to the non-ordinary locus, and the ordinary locus is dense in each component of the special fibre. So the rank jumps and the map is not flat.

The paper never uses integral flatness:
- p. 987 says the maps are finite étale on the good-reduction generic fibre;
- Corollary 3.2.22(i) claims only that ϕ[1/p] is finite and flat, and factors ϕ = τ∘ψ with τ not an isomorphism integrally;
- the traces in Corollary 3.2.23 are taken after inverting p.

sourceIssues.printed: The source defines Γ_0(p^m) = {γ ∈ GSp_{2g}(ℤ_p) | γ ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 ∗) mod p^m, det γ ≡ 1 mod p^m}. It describes the added requirement det γ ≡ 1 mod p^m as slightly nonstandard, and uses the symplectic similitude factor to assert that X*_{Γ_0(p^m)} is naturally over ℚ(ζ_{p^m}).
sourceIssues.correction: The extra condition should be on the similitude factor, c(γ) ≡ 1 mod p^m, where γ^tJγ = c(γ)J. Then c(Γ_0(p^m)) = 1 + p^mℤ_p and X*_{Γ_0(p^m)} is naturally a ℚ(ζ_{p^m})-scheme.
sourceIssues.reason:
For γ ∈ GSp_{2g}, det γ = c(γ)^g. So the printed condition gives c(Γ_0(p^m)) = {c ∈ ℤ_p^× : c^g ≡ 1 mod p^m}; every such c occurs, e.g. via γ = diag(1,…,1,c,…,c).

This is larger than 1 + p^mℤ_p whenever x ↦ x^g is not injective on (ℤ/p^m)^×. For example, take g = 2, p odd and γ = diag(1,1,−1,−1): it is block upper-triangular with c(γ) = −1 and det γ = 1.

The similitude factor on X_{Γ_0(p^m)} is then determined only up to such c, so there is no tautological ζ_{p^m}, and X*_{Γ_0(p^m)} is not naturally over ℚ(ζ_{p^m}). The paper needs that structure: p. 983 defines 𝒳_{K_p} from X_{K_p} ⊗_{ℚ(ζ_{p^m})} ℚ_p^cycl 'using the tautological element ζ_{p^m} ∈ ℚ_p^cycl and ζ_{p^m} ∈ 𝒪_{X_{K_p}}, given by the symplectic similitude factor'.

The context makes the intended condition clear. For g = 1 the two conditions agree. Extraction item 26 reproduces 'det γ'; see itemChanges.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.3.2, proof of Corollary 2.3.5, p. 963 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary II.3.5, p. 20. Same text in both.
sourceIssues.printed: The source says it must still establish the almost-isomorphism property for A → Hom_{A_0^{1/p^∞}}(g^{1/p^∞}A_0^{1/p^∞}, A). It claims the explicit expression for A and the u^i basis reduce this to the next lemma.
sourceIssues.correction:
The reduction to Lemma 2.3.6 needs a bound that is uniform in i.

The bound: take C ∈ ℤ_{≥0} with C·v(f) ≥ v(g) for the finitely many height-one primes containing f. Then, by normality of the A_0^{1/p^n}, g^e m ∈ fA_0^{1/p^∞} implies f^{Ce} m ∈ fA_0^{1/p^∞}.

Now let φ ∈ Hom(J, A) and choose k with C/p^k ≤ ε. Then (uf)^{C/p^k}φ is supported on finitely many u^i, namely those near the support of φ(g^{1/p^k}). Lemma 2.3.6 then applies to finitely many summands. The corollary stands.
sourceIssues.reason:
J = g^{1/p^∞}A_0^{1/p^∞} is not finitely generated, so Hom(J, ⊕_i M_i) = lim_k ⊕_i M_i, with transition maps multiplication by g^{1/p^k − 1/p^{k+1}}. This can be strictly larger than ⊕_i Hom(J, M_i), which is all that Lemma 2.3.6 controls.

Example, within the corollary's hypotheses: A_0 = 𝔽_p[x,y], f = x, g = xy. Define φ(g^{1/p^k}) = Σ_{j=1}^{k−1} x^{1+1/p^k−1/p^j} y^{1/p^k} u^{j+1}. It is compatible:
- g^{1/p^k−1/p^{k+1}}φ(g^{1/p^{k+1}}) = φ(g^{1/p^k});
- the new j = k term becomes x·y^{1/p^k}u^{k+1} = 0, since f·u^i = 0 for i ≥ 1.
Its u-support is unbounded, so φ is not in the image of A. It is only almost in the image: (uf)^ε φ has finite support.

I checked the bound in the correction with divisorial valuations on the normal noetherian A_0^{1/p^n}; the proof of Lemma 2.3.6 (p. 965) uses the same kind of constant C.

sourceIssues.printed: The source characterizes ordinary B by B[p^∞] ≅ (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^g × μ^g_{p^∞}. sourceIssues.locator: §4.2, proof of Corollary 4.2.3, p. 1024 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary IV.2.3, p. 72
sourceIssues.printed: Assuming failure of the last statement, the source selects the largest violating codimension c among the H̃_i, then the smallest i < d attaining c. It asserts codim H̃_i = c < d − i and codim H̃_k > c when k < i. It claims E^j(H̃_k) vanishes when j < c with j + k < d, since otherwise codim H̃_k ≤ j < c together with j + k < d would contradict the selection of c.
sourceIssues.correction: choose the minimal one, c (the minimal codimension among the H̃_i with i < d and codim H̃_i < d − i).
sourceIssues.reason: Call H̃_k violating if k < d and codim H̃_k < d − k. With c the maximal violating codimension, neither step of the proof holds. First, a violating H̃_k with k < i has codimension ≤ c and ≠ c (i is minimal), so < c; this contradicts 'the codimension of H̃_k for k < i is greater than c'. Second, 'codim H̃_k ≤ j < c' is no contradiction with a maximal c. That second step is what kills the differentials d_r : E_r^{c−r,i+r−1} → E_r^{c,i} into the codimension-c term (their sources have j = c − r < c and j + k = i + c − 1 < d), so the argument needs it. With c minimal both steps hold. For k < i, a violating H̃_k has codimension ≥ c and ≠ c; a non-violating one has codimension ≥ d − k > d − i > c. A nonzero E^j(H̃_k) with j < c and j + k < d would make H̃_k violating with codimension ≤ j < c. The targets E^{c+r}(H̃_{i−r+1}) have codimension ≥ c + r in any case (Venjakob). So a codimension-c subquotient of E^c(H̃_i) survives into H̃^BM_{2d−i−c} = 0, the intended contradiction. Checked on a render of the published page and in the v2 TeX.

sourceIssues.printed: Corollary 5.1.11 takes T_cl from Theorem 4.3.1 and asserts that every continuous quotient T_cl → A with discrete A admits a unique continuous h-dimensional G_{F,S}-determinant D valued in A. The proof says the open ideal I = ker(T_cl → A) includes an intersection of finitely many I_{K,k} = ker(T_cl → T_{K,k}), by the topology’s definition, and treats this as proving the result.
sourceIssues.correction: Take T_cl = T_{cl,m} with m > n if F is totally real and m ≥ n if F is CM. With this hypothesis every weight mk (k ≥ 1) in the topology is in the range of Corollaries 5.1.7/5.1.10.
sourceIssues.reason: Theorem 4.3.1 fixes an arbitrary integer m ≥ 1 and topologizes T by the maps to End(H^0(𝒳*_{K_pK^p}, ω^{⊗mk} ⊗ ℐ)) for all k ≥ 1, so weight m itself occurs. sourceIssues.printed: The source chooses the smallest k for which not every Q_m satisfies Q_m ≡ 1 mod X^k. It then asserts Q_m ≡ 1 + (XT^m)^k a_m mod X^{k+1}, with a_m ∈ S and all but finitely many a_m zero.
sourceIssues.correction: Let k ≥ 1 be maximal such that all Q_m ≡ 1 mod X^k (equivalently, minimal such that not all Q_m ≡ 1 mod X^{k+1}).
sourceIssues.reason: If k is minimal with not all Q_m ≡ 1 mod X^k, then not all Q_m are ≡ 1 mod X^k. But the next formula, Q_m ≡ 1 + (XT^m)^k a_m mod X^{k+1}, forces every Q_m ≡ 1 mod X^k. Off by one; with the corrected k, the no-cancellation argument among the T^{mk} is as printed.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.3, proof of Lemma 5.3.10 (the claim Q_m ∈ S[XT^m]), pp. 1053–1054 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Lemma V.3.10, p. 98
sourceIssues.printed: The source places Q′ in S[[X, XT]], hence in S[T][[X]], and states Q′Q_0 ∈ S[T, X]. It expands Q′ = Σ_{a≥0} Q′_a(T)X^a with coefficients Q′_a(T) ∈ S[T], asserting Q′_aQ_0 = 0 once a is sufficiently large. Since Q_0 ∈ S[T] has 1 as its constant coefficient, it concludes Q′_a = 0 and therefore Q′ ∈ S[T, X].
sourceIssues.correction: Swap the roles of X and T: Q′ ∈ S[[T, XT]], so Q′ ∈ S[X][[T]]; write Q′ = Σ_{a≥0} Q′_a(X)T^a with Q′_a(X) ∈ S[X]; then Q′_aQ_0 is the T^a-coefficient of Q′Q_0 = Q, hence 0 for a large, and as Q_0 ∈ S[X] has constant coefficient 1 (so is a non-zero-divisor) Q′_a = 0.
sourceIssues.reason: Here Q_m = 1 for m < 0 and Q′ = ∏_{m>0} Q_m with Q_m ∈ S[[XT^m]]. For m ≥ 2, XT^m ∉ S[[X, XT]], since monomials X^{i+j}T^j there have T-degree at most their X-degree; but XT^m = T^{m−1}(XT) ∈ S[[T, XT]]. The paragraph before establishes Q_0 ∈ S[X] ('Q ≡ Q_0 mod T so, in particular, Q_0 ∈ S[X]'), so 'Q_0 ∈ S[T]' contradicts it. In the printed X-expansion the X^a-coefficient of Q′Q_0 is Σ_b c_bQ′_{a−b}(T), where Q_0 = Σ c_bX^b, not Q′_aQ_0, so the step fails as written. After the swap it is correct.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.3, proof of Lemma 5.3.8 (multiplicativity of D^{(m)}), the display before Lemma 5.3.12, p. 1055 (published); arXiv v2: p. 99
sourceIssues.printed: The source invokes the multiplicity of D_0^{(m)} to express the target identity as D_0^{(m)}((1 − U(x + y) + Uxy)(1 + Ux + U²x² + ⋯)(1 + Uy + U²y² + ⋯))|_{U=1} = 1. It sets f = (1 − U(x + y) + Uxy)(1 + Ux + U²x² + ⋯)(1 + Uy + U²y² + ⋯) ∈ 1 + US[G][U], reducing multiplicativity of D^{(m)} to the subsequent lemma.
sourceIssues.correction: f = (1 − U(x + y) + Uxy)(1 + Uy + U²y² + ⋯)(1 + Ux + U²x² + ⋯), i.e. multiply by (1 − Uy)^{−1} before (1 − Ux)^{−1}.
sourceIssues.reason: Lemma 5.3.12 requires f|_{U=1} = 1. S[G] is non-commutative when G is (in the application G = Gal(F̃/F)), and the printed f has f|_{U=1} = (1 − x)(1 − y)(1 − x)^{−1}(1 − y)^{−1}, a commutator. Example: x = εg, y = δh with ε² = δ² = 0 and gh ≠ hg gives f|_{U=1} = 1 + εδ(gh − hg) ≠ 1. With the factors reversed, f|_{U=1} = (1 − x)(1 − y)(1 − y)^{−1}(1 − x)^{−1} = 1 and still f ≡ 1 mod I. Since D_0^{(m)} is multiplicative with commutative values, D_0^{(m)}(f) does not depend on the order, so the desired equation is unchanged and the reduction works. ('multiplicity' is also a slip for 'multiplicativity'.)

sourceIssues.locator: §5.4, proof of Corollary 5.4.2, p. 1059 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary V.4.2, p. 103
sourceIssues.printed: The source says that a twist by a character 𝔸_F^× → ℤ/2ℤ, whose archimedean components are prescribed, makes π′ occur in H^i(X_K, ℳ_{ξ,K}) ⊗_{ℤ̄_p} ℂ. It adopts this occurrence as an assumption for the remaining argument.
sourceIssues.correction: Allow the quadratic character η to ramify at an auxiliary finite set S′ of places disjoint from S. Run the argument with S ∪ S′ to get σ_{π⊗η}, and put σ_π = σ_{π⊗η} ⊗ η^{−1}. Doing this for two choices of η with disjoint auxiliary sets, and comparing by Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt, shows that σ_π is unramified outside S.
sourceIssues.reason: For π′⊗η to occur at a level K = K_SK^S, η must be unramified outside S. A quadratic Hecke character with prescribed archimedean components that is unramified outside S need not exist. Example: F = ℚ, p = 5, S = {5}, n = 1, π = π′|·|^{−1} with π′ an odd character of order 4 and conductor 5 (regular L-algebraic, unramified outside S). Here X̃_K ≅ Ẑ^×/K and X_K ≅ Ẑ^×/{±1}K (K_5 = 1 + 5ℤ_5, K_ℓ = ℤ_ℓ^× for ℓ ≠ 5), so π′ occurs in H^0(X̃_K) but not in H^0(X_K), which sees only even characters. The only quadratic characters of ℚ^×\𝔸^× unramified outside 5 are 1 and the character of ℚ(√5), and both are even, so no admissible twist exists. The statement of Corollary 5.4.2 is unaffected; its proof needs the repair.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.4, proof of Corollary 5.4.2, p. 1060 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary V.4.2, p. 103
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts that the first kernel is contained in the second for the maps T_{F,S} → T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i) and T_{F,S} → ∏_{m≥1} T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i, m), respectively. Invoking Theorem 5.4.1 together with [19, Example 2.32], it deduces a continuous determinant D of G_{F,S}, of dimension n, valued in T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i)/I with I nilpotent.
sourceIssues.correction: The true containment is the reverse: ker(T_{F,S} → ∏_m T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i, m)) ⊂ ker(T_{F,S} → T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i)). So T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i) is a quotient of B = im(T_{F,S} → ∏_m T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i, m)). Theorem 5.4.1 (N uniform in m) and [19, Example 2.32] give a determinant on B/(B ∩ ∏_m I_m), whose ideal has N-th power 0. Its push-forward along B ↠ T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i) is a determinant with values in T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i)/Ī, with Ī^N = 0.
sourceIssues.reason: Put H^i = H^i(X_K, ℳ_{ξ,K}). There is a Hecke-equivariant exact sequence 0 → H^i/p^m → H^i(X_K, ℳ_{ξ,K}/p^m) → H^{i+1}[p^m] → 0. An operator killing every H^i(X_K, ℳ/p^m) kills every H^i/p^m, hence kills H^i (H^i is finitely generated over a finite extension of ℤ_p, so ∩_m p^mH^i = 0); this gives the reverse containment. The printed containment would need an operator killing H^i to kill H^{i+1}[p^m] too. That fails whenever a Hecke eigensystem occurs in the torsion of H^{i+1} but not in H^i. Example in the setting of Theorem 5.4.1, which allows stacky levels: F = ℚ, n = 1, p = 2, K = Ẑ^×, i = 1. Then X_K = [pt/{±1}], H^1(X_K, ℤ_2) = 0 and H^1(X_K, ℤ/2) = ℤ/2, so the first kernel is all of T and the second is not. The same step recurs in the proof of Corollary 5.4.4 and in footnote 29; Remark 5.4.5 calls the result for im(T → ∏_m …) 'slightly stronger', which is consistent only with the corrected direction. The stated results, including I^N = 0, remain true.
